patient.chief_complaint: Progressive right-sided headaches, left arm weakness, and a first-time seizure
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Paolo Feretti is a 59-year-old right-handed man and avid amateur cyclist who presents to the emergency department following a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His wife reports that approximately four weeks ago he began experiencing intermittent tingling and burning pain in his left hand and forearm. Initially, he and his general practitioner attributed these symptoms to nerve compression related to prolonged cycling posture on his road bike, and he was referred for physiotherapy. Over the following two weeks, the paresthesias became more frequent and intense, occurring not only during cycling but also at rest, and were accompanied by brief involuntary twitching movements of his left hand lasting seconds at a time. Three weeks ago, he developed a progressive right-sided headache that was worst in the early morning hours and occasionally woke him from sleep. Over-the-counter ibuprofen provided only partial relief. Approximately two weeks ago, his wife began noticing that he had difficulty using his left hand for fine motor tasks such as buttoning shirts and typing on his keyboard. He also appeared more forgetful and slower in his thinking over the past ten days, occasionally losing track of conversations and misplacing items. This morning at approximately 08:30, while sitting at the breakfast table, his wife witnessed his left hand begin to assume a tonic posture, followed within seconds by rhythmic clonic jerking that spread to involve the entire left arm and then progressed to a generalized convulsion lasting approximately 75 seconds. He was confused and somnolent for about ten minutes afterward. EMS was called and he was transported to the emergency department. On arrival, he was alert and conversant but had a persistent right-sided headache and mild left arm weakness. He denies any prior seizure history, recent head trauma, fever, vision changes, nausea, or vomiting. He reports no recent weight loss or night sweats. A non-contrast CT scan obtained in the emergency department demonstrated a large heterogeneously hyperdense mass in the right frontal lobe with significant surrounding hypodensity suggestive of vasogenic edema and approximately 9 mm of leftward midline shift. He was started on intravenous dexamethasone and levetiracetam, and admitted to the neurology service for further evaluation.

signal_characteristics.post_gadolinium: Thick, irregular ring enhancement with multiple nodular enhancing components, most prominent along the medial and inferior margins; no enhancement within the necrotic core

tissue_diagnosis.site: as targeted on the contrast-enhancing rim
tissue_diagnosis.histological_diagnosis: Highly cellular glial neoplasm with marked nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity (>10 mitoses per 10 HPF), microvascular proliferation, and large areas of pseudopalisading necrosis
tissue_diagnosis.impression: Integrated diagnosis: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4. The layered report is what the WHO CNS5 classification requires — histology, grade and molecular findings combined — and it is what converts a radiological suspicion into a diagnosis that determines treatment. Imaging cannot substitute for it, and the molecular result changes the protocol, not merely the label.

output.query: glioblastoma standard treatment protocol Stupp temozolomide

results.title: Radiotherapy plus concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide for glioblastoma
results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.summary: Landmark trial establishing the Stupp protocol: maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with concurrent daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2) followed by 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, 5/28 days). Improved median OS from 12.1 to 14.6 months. MGMT methylation predicted benefit.

results.title: Effects of radiotherapy with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide versus radiotherapy alone on survival in glioblastoma: 5-year follow-up
results.authors: Stupp R, Hegi ME, Mason WP, et al.
results.summary: Long-term follow-up confirmed durable survival benefit with combined chemoradiation. 5-year OS rate 9.8% vs 1.9% with radiotherapy alone. MGMT promoter methylation associated with strongest benefit (median OS 21.7 vs 15.3 months for unmethylated).

results.title: Tumor treating fields plus maintenance temozolomide for glioblastoma: the EF-14 trial
results.authors: Stupp R, Taillibert S, Kanner A, et al.
results.summary: Addition of tumor treating fields (TTFields) to maintenance temozolomide improved median PFS (6.7 vs 4.0 months) and OS (20.9 vs 16.0 months) compared to temozolomide alone.

differential.key_features: No known primary cancer; staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis negative; infiltrative margins and corpus-callosum or eloquent-cortex involvement more typical of primary glioma than metastasis
In immunocompetent patients typically presents as homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass with diffuse DWI restriction and no central necrosis; ring enhancement with necrosis argues against
No fever or leukocytosis; DWI restriction at the enhancing rim (not centrally as in pyogenic pus) and elevated rCBV are inconsistent with abscess
Closed ring enhancement, marked mass effect, and central necrosis are atypical for tumefactive MS; demyelinating lesions usually show incomplete ('open') ring enhancement on the cortical side

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiogram has no role in the diagnostic workup of suspected high-grade glioma absent a specific cardiac question (e.g., suspected paraneoplastic endocarditis)
Cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic workup of a brain mass and adds resource cost without informing management

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in suspected intracranial mass with significant midline shift (9 mm): the pressure gradient created by LP risks transtentorial or tonsillar herniation. Even when LP is otherwise safe, CSF studies are low-yield for primary brain tumor diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: MRI must precede any lumbar puncture when a mass lesion is suspected, to identify mass effect and herniation risk before LP
Imaging plans the approach and identifies the enhancing target to sample; biopsying before it risks a non-diagnostic specimen from a necrotic centre

critical_actions: Obtain urgent neurosurgical consultation for tissue diagnosis (stereotactic biopsy or maximal safe resection) and operative planning
Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) before any invasive procedure
Administer dexamethasone (loading dose 10 mg IV, then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce vasogenic edema and mass effect (9 mm midline shift)
Initiate antiepileptic therapy with levetiracetam (preferred non-enzyme-inducing AED) for documented seizure activity
Obtain pre-operative labs (CBC, BMP, coagulation, type & screen) before craniotomy/biopsy
Plan multimodal treatment per molecular and histological profile (e.g., Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation with temozolomide for IDH-wildtype GBM)
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture in the setting of mass effect (9 mm midline shift) — herniation risk
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
key_reasoning_points: Combination of progressive headache (worse mornings), new focal neurological deficit, and/or new-onset seizure in an adult is a high-risk presentation requiring urgent contrast-enhanced brain MRI

MRI features of a right frontal heterogeneously / ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, perilesional FLAIR-hyperintense edema, restricted diffusion at the enhancing rim, and mass effect are characteristic of high-grade glioma
Perfusion MRI (elevated rCBV) and MR spectroscopy (elevated Cho/NAA, lipid-lactate) corroborate high-grade neoplasm and help guide biopsy targeting
Significant midline shift / herniation risk mandates urgent dexamethasone and neurosurgical evaluation; lumbar puncture is contraindicated
Definitive diagnosis requires tissue (stereotactic biopsy or surgical resection) with molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, 1p/19q, TERT, H3K27M); imaging alone cannot substitute for histology
For IDH-wildtype GBM, current standard of care is maximal safe resection followed by the Stupp protocol (concurrent radiation + temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide)

Avoid ordering off-pathway advanced-imaging modalities (DaTscan, amyloid PET, FDG-PET, carotid duplex, transcranial Doppler) — they address other neurological differentials and add cost without informing glioma management
New-onset focal or generalized seizure with a focal-onset mass mandates AED therapy (levetiracetam preferred — non-enzyme-inducing, fewer interactions with temozolomide)

metadata.difficulty_description: Straightforward presentation with classic findings: progressive headache, contralateral motor deficit, and new-onset seizure in a middle-aged adult with CT showing a large enhancing mass with midline shift. MRI findings are textbook for glioblastoma with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, and surrounding edema. Minimal confounders.
